```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rolescry)
set.seed(1)
```

## The problem: names lie, data does not

Real datasets arrive with column names that are missing, misleading, in the
wrong language, or simply wrong: a column called `category_code` holding
continuous lab values, a `gender` column that is actually a free numeric
measurement, an outcome buried under an opaque `v7`. Any tool that decides a
column's statistical *role* from its **name** inherits every one of those lies.

`rolescry` decides roles from the **data signature** instead -- the guiding
principle is *Data inspice, non nomen* ("inspect the data, not the name").
Renaming every column to `col_1, col_2, ...` does not change a single role
assignment. This is the **turnusol** (litmus) invariant, and it is the
package's keystone test.

## A worked example

```{r example}
set.seed(1)
pre  <- rnorm(100, 10, 2)          # a measurement, before ...
d <- data.frame(
  arm  = rep(c("control", "treatment"), each = 50),  # a balanced 2-level grouping
  pre  = pre,
  post = pre + rnorm(100, 1, 1)                       # ... and again after (paired with pre)
)

res <- detect_roles(d)
res
summary(res)
```

The same call on the name-stripped twin yields the same roles by position:

```{r blind}
d_blind <- setNames(d, paste0("col_", seq_along(d)))
pos <- function(r, dat) match(r$roles$paired_pairs$columns, names(dat))
identical(pos(detect_roles(d), d), pos(detect_roles(d_blind), d_blind))
```

## How a role is scored

Each column is first **typed by value** (`continuous`, `binary`, `categorical`,
`ID`), never by name. Candidate roles are then scored by signatures that capture
the statistical shape a role implies. Group variables are ranked by normalized
entropy; paired versus agreement measurements are separated by whether the
difference carries a systematic shift (a description-length criterion); ordinal
scale items by a one-factor description-length code; survival, wide repeated
measures and binary scale items still use point signatures (event-rate and
right-skew, same-units correlation blocks, item endorsement). Every score is a
transparent set of named components you can inspect (bits for derived roles,
points for the rest):

```{r breakdown}
res$roles$paired_pairs$components[[1]]
```

### Shannon entropy

For a categorical column with level proportions \(p_1, \dots, p_k\), the
normalized Shannon entropy

\[ H_{\text{norm}} = \frac{-\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i}{\log_2 k} \in [0, 1] \]

measures how balanced the levels are. A grouping variable (treatment vs control)
has high entropy (near-balanced); a near-constant flag has entropy near zero.
Entropy drives both the value classifier and the group-balance signal.

### Normalized mutual information

To ask -- name-blind -- whether a candidate grouping actually *carries
information about* an outcome, `rolescry` uses normalized mutual information:

\[ \text{NMI}(X, Y) = \frac{I(X; Y)}{\min\{H(X),\, H(Y)\}} \in [0, 1], \]

which is 0 for independent variables and 1 for a deterministic association, and
is comparable across variables with different numbers of levels. It is exposed
directly:

```{r nmi}
set.seed(2)
g <- sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 300, replace = TRUE)
y <- ifelse(g == "A", "event", sample(c("event", "none"), 300, replace = TRUE))
compute_nmi(g, y)          # > 0: g informs y
compute_nmi(g, sample(g))  # ~ 0: shuffled -> independent
```

## Honesty under ambiguity (0.3.0)

Some role questions have no answer in the data alone. A dependent pair of one
binary and one positive continuous column is equally readable as a survival
(time, event) pair or as a (cause, outcome) pair; `rolescry` assigns the
survival roles only when the censoring geometry singles that reading out, and
otherwise reports the pair *as a pair* and leaves the interpretation to you:

```{r coupled}
set.seed(3)
n <- 300; arm <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2)
end <- rnorm(n, 150, 15) - 10 * arm
rct <- data.frame(arm = arm, sbp_end = end,
                  resp = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.05 * (end - 140))))
cp <- detect_roles(rct)$roles$coupled_pair
cp$columns
cp$interpretations
```

## Beyond one domain

The signatures are domain-free, so the same call reads financial, social or
experimental tables. Calendar columns (`Date`/`POSIXct`, or character columns
whose every value parses as a date) are reported as `time_index`; a balanced
long panel whose entity/time axes are value-symmetric is reported as
axis-ambiguous (`repeated_measures$panel_axes`) unless serial dependence of the
measures singles one reading out:

```{r finance}
set.seed(5)
px <- data.frame(dt = as.Date("2024-01-02") + 0:199,
                 price = 500 + cumsum(rnorm(200)), volume = rlnorm(200, 11, 0.5))
detect_roles(px)$roles$time_index$columns
```

A finance keyword dictionary is available for the capped name channel:
`rolescry_default_name_bonus("finance")` (or `"all"` for the union with the
clinical dictionary).

## The optional, capped name bonus

Names are not *useless* -- they are just untrustworthy. When you do trust them,
pass a keyword dictionary via `name_bonus`. Names then act only as a small,
**capped** tie-breaker (at most a +10 point nudge, i.e. <= 10% of the selection
score); the mathematical signature still dominates (>= 90%), the relationship
enforced by `score_gap_ok()`.

Here two columns both look like groupings; the data alone picks the perfectly
balanced `site`, but a keyword dictionary nudges the choice to the intended
treatment arm:

```{r namebonus}
set.seed(4)
clin <- data.frame(
  site    = rep(c("north", "south"), length.out = 160),  # perfectly balanced (the math pick)
  treated = sample(c("no", "yes"), 160, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.62, 0.38))
)
detect_roles(clin)$roles$group_var$columns                                  # data alone -> "site"
detect_roles(clin, name_bonus = rolescry_default_name_bonus())$roles$group_var$columns  # name nudge -> "treated"
```

## Verifying a declared analysis plan

`verify_roles()` asks whether the data can support a role assignment you declare.
Here the claim wrongly pairs `age` with `sbp_end`; the real pre/post pair is left out.

```{r verify}
set.seed(21); n <- 300
arm <- rep(c("drug", "placebo"), each = n / 2)
base <- rnorm(n, 150, 15)
rct <- data.frame(id = sample.int(99999, n), arm, age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 10)),
                  sbp_base = base, sbp_end = base - 10 * (arm == "drug") + rnorm(n, 0, 8))
rct$y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 0.05 * (rct$sbp_end - 140)))
verify_roles(rct, list(subject_id = "id", group_var = "arm", paired_pairs = c("age", "sbp_end"),
                       outcome_binary = "y"))
```

The paired claim is `contradicted`: `age` and `sbp_end` share no information beyond the
noise floor, a falsification backed by a value statistic. `id` is `consistent`
as a subject identifier (all values distinct). The two design claims
are `unverifiable(identifiability)`: which column is the grouping or the outcome
is a design fact the joint distribution cannot reveal, so the data never call it
`consistent`. A `consistent` verdict elsewhere means only "a reading the data
support", never "correct", and `unverifiable(coverage)` means the package has no
test or the evidence is empty. The last block lists the real pair
`sbp_base`/`sbp_end`, which the claim did not mention.

## Aligning roles across sites

Pooling data from several centers starts with finding which column plays which role
in each file. `harmonize_roles(sites)` runs the name-blind detector on every site and
tabulates, per role, the column each site holds (`aligned` = found everywhere,
`partial`, `absent`). Here the two sites share no column names and the order differs,
and the event is coded 0/1 at one site and 1/2 at the other.

```{r harmonize}
site <- function(seed, nm, n = 200, code = 0:1) {
  set.seed(seed); b <- rnorm(n, 150, 15); t <- rweibull(n, 1.3, exp(5 - rnorm(n)))
  cens <- runif(n, 0, quantile(t, .9))
  d <- data.frame(sample.int(99999, n), sample(c("a", "b"), n, TRUE), b, b - 5 + rnorm(n, 0, 6),
                  round(pmin(t, cens), 1), code[1 + (t <= cens)])
  setNames(d, nm)
}
north <- site(1, c("id", "arm", "sbp_base", "sbp_end", "time", "dead"))
south <- site(2, c("pid", "group", "bp0", "bp1", "ftime", "status"), code = 1:2)[, c(3, 1, 6, 2, 5, 4)]
harmonize_roles(list(north = north, south = south))
```
* `map` is the table above; `checks` adds descriptive rows per role found in two or
  more sites (value type, event levels and coding, group-label Jaccard, range and
  range overlap, battery size); `site_only` lists roles found at one site only.
* Only categorical facts are flagged: `type_mismatch`, `coding_mismatch` (the
  normalized event coding differs: 0/1, 1/2 and TRUE/FALSE normalize to the same
  two-level shape, which level is the event is not checked; a 0/1/2 status differs) and `size_mismatch` (item counts differ). Jaccard and range overlap are
  reported, never flagged, and no numeric threshold decides a flag.
* Alignment is by role only; names appear in the output cells. The residual
  `covariate` role is excluded.
* `aligned` means the detector found the role at every site; it does not establish that the columns measure the same thing; read `checks` (levels, Jaccard, ranges) before pooling. Cell order is alphabetical and carries no pairing direction.

## Header-aware loading

`read_data()` reads a file with the header row found by the same
information-theoretic scorer (`detect_header()`), so messy exports with title
rows or merged cells still load with sensible column names. Delimited text works
with base R; spreadsheet and statistical formats use optional packages and
degrade gracefully if they are not installed.
